passages.t: The LORD answers out of the whirlwind
passages.happening:
‘Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said’ (verse 1): “Who is this who obscures My counsel by words without knowledge? Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me” (verses 2-3).

“Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding. Who fixed its measurements? Surely you know! Or who stretched a measuring line across it? On what were its foundations set, or who laid its cornerstone, while the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?” (verses 4-7).

Who shut in the sea behind doors when it burst out of the womb, when God made the clouds its garment and darkness its blanket, set its bounds and told it how far it could come, ‘here your proud waves must stop’ (verse 11)?
passages.hearers:
This is the moment the whole book has waited for. Job has demanded a hearing again and again, most recently when he signed his defense and asked the Almighty to answer (31:35). The friends and Elihu have spoken for God. Now God speaks for himself. For the first time since the prologue, the narrator names the speaker with the covenant name, the LORD.

The setting is a courtroom turned inside out. Job had wanted to question God. Now God tells Job to brace himself, literally to gird up his loins, tucking his long robe into his belt for hard work, and to answer as the one questioned. The reversal is not cruel but clarifying. Job had spoken as though he could see the whole case.

The world is pictured as a building, with foundations, measurements, a cornerstone, and the sea as a force held behind doors and bars, the shared picture of the world in the ancient Near East. Counsel, etsah, means God's purposes in governing the world. Job's error was not asking questions but speaking as though he understood God's design.

The whirlwind, searah, is a storm that overwhelms, and yet out of it God speaks to one man by name.
passages.later: The same storm word is used when Elijah is taken up: ‘and Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind’ (2 Kings 2:11).
passages.hard:
Why does God not explain Job's suffering? Is this speech simply overpowering him?

Many readers feel this. Job asked why he was suffering, and God answers with questions about the stars and the sea. Some critics have read the speech as a display of raw power that silences Job without answering him.

Others, reading the book as a whole, see several things happening. First, the speech is not hostile. God comes, speaks personally, and talks about his care for creatures no one else notices. Second, it corrects the idea Job and his friends shared, that the world runs by a simple rule of reward and punishment that humans can inspect. The world God describes is vast and wild, ordered by a wisdom beyond human sight. Third, in the epilogue God says that Job has spoken rightly of him, which suggests the speech is not a condemnation.

The book never says that the reasons for suffering cannot be known in principle. It shows that Job did not know them, that God did, and that meeting God proved enough for Job even without the explanation. The speeches never mention the test in heaven. Readers who want a theory of suffering from this chapter will not find one. They will find a God who comes.

The same is true for any reader in pain. God's answer to Job does not explain anyone's particular loss, and no one should use it to silence a person who is asking why.
passages.asks: God answered Job with questions. Ask what questions God might ask you, if you stood where Job stood. And ask whether you could find, as Job did, that meeting God matters more than being given the reason.

passages.t: Morning, the deep, and the storehouses of snow
passages.happening:
“In your days, have you commanded the morning or assigned the dawn its place, that it might spread to the ends of the earth and shake the wicked out of it?” (verses 12-13). The earth takes shape at dawn like clay under a seal.

Has Job walked the depths of the sea? “Have the gates of death been revealed to you? Have you seen the gates of the shadow of death?” (verse 17). Does he know where light lives and where darkness has its home? “Surely you know, for you were already born! And the number of your days is great!” (verse 21).

“Have you entered the storehouses of snow or observed the storehouses of hail” (verse 22)? Who cuts a channel for the flood and a path for the thunderbolt, ‘to bring rain on a barren land, on a desert where no man lives’ (verse 26)? “Does the rain have a father? Who has begotten the drops of dew?” (verse 28). From whose womb does the ice come, when the waters turn hard as stone?
passages.hearers:
The speech moves through the world in a rough order: the founding of the earth, the sea, the morning, the depths and the realm of the dead, light and darkness, then snow, hail, lightning, rain and ice.

The dawn spreading across the earth is pictured like a seal pressed into clay, bringing out the shape of the hills, and like a cloth shaken, so that the wicked who work at night are shaken out of it.

Notice verse 26. God sends rain on a desert where no one lives. Much of the speech concerns places humans never go and things that serve no human purpose. Ancient thought often pictured the world as ordered for the service of the gods or for human use. God's speech describes a world far larger than human interests, full of things he tends simply because he made them.

Verse 21 is irony. Job, who is not as old as the world, cannot know these things.
passages.asks: God sends rain where no one will ever see it. Ask whether you believe God's care reaches places and people you will never see. And ask what it does to your complaint, or your pride, to remember how small your view is.

passages.t: The stars, the clouds, and the raven's young
passages.happening:
“Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loosen the belt of Orion? Can you bring forth the constellations in their seasons or lead out the Bear and her cubs? Do you know the laws of the heavens?” (verses 31-33).

Can Job command the clouds or send the lightning on its way? ‘Who has put wisdom in the heart or given understanding to the mind?’ (verse 36). Who can count the clouds or tip the water jars of the sky when the dust is caked hard?

“Can you hunt the prey for a lioness or satisfy the hunger of young lions when they crouch in their dens and lie in wait in the thicket? Who provides food for the raven when its young cry out to God as they wander about for lack of food?” (verses 39-41).
passages.hearers:
The star names were known across the ancient world. Kimah is usually identified as the Pleiades and kesil as Orion. The Bear and her cubs is less certain, and the word for constellations in verse 32, mazzaroth, is found only here and its meaning is debated.

Then the speech turns to the animals, and it begins with hunger. God feeds the lioness's cubs and the raven's young. The raven was an unclean bird under Israel's law, and still God feeds it when its young cry out to him.

The whole chapter is questions, most of them with no answer Job could give. They are not meant to humiliate him. They are meant to show him the size of the world God holds, and the tenderness with which he holds it.
passages.later: The prophet Amos praises the same Maker, ‘He who made the Pleiades and Orion’ (Amos 5:8). And a psalm says what verse 41 asks: “He provides food for the animals, and for the young ravens when they call” (Psalm 147:9).
passages.asks: God feeds young ravens when they cry out to him. Ask whether you believe he hears your cries as he hears theirs. And ask who near you is crying out for food, of any kind, and whether you could be part of God's answer.
